vecchio: title: "GPU-accelerated single-cell and spatial transcriptomics on NVIDIA DGX H100: a systematic benchmark of speed, scalability, and biological concordance"
nuovo: title: "GPU-accelerated single-cell (NVIDIA DGX H100) and spatial (RTX 4090) transcriptomics: per-step speedups, capacity and concordance against a 100-CPU reference"
nota: Titolo opzione A di scelte_R1.md (hardware per modalita', senza 'systematic' e 'scalability'; 'capacity' invece di 'memory limits', log SLURM 16531/16463/16662); difflib ratio 0.590 contro il titolo dello short paper. Riportare lo stesso titolo nel LaTeX e in METEOR (S7).

vecchio: **Abstract.** Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) datasets now routinely exceed one million cells, and spatial transcriptomics platforms such as Visium HD generate hundreds of thousands of measurement bins per tissue section, placing severe computational demands on analysis frameworks that remain predominantly CPU-bound. We present a systematic benchmark comparing Scanpy (CPU, 100 cores) against rapids-singlecell (GPU, 1-8 NVIDIA H100 80 GB) on the 1.3-million mouse brain cell dataset, evaluating speed, multi-GPU scalability, memory efficiency, and biological concordance across five dataset sizes (10k-1.3M cells) with five independent repeats. The GPU pipeline achieved up to 120-fold end-to-end speedup at 1.3M cells (435 s vs 52,056 s on CPU), reducing a 14.5-hour analysis to 7.3 minutes. Biological concordance was high: HVG selection was identical (Jaccard = 1.0), PCA loadings perfectly correlated (Spearman |rho| = 1.0), and Leiden clustering concordance ranged from ARI = 0.908 to 0.963. Multi-GPU scaling was sublinear due to CPU preprocessing dominance. A memory-optimised pipeline processed 11.9 million cells on a single DGX H100 node, with CPU RAM as the binding constraint (GPU VRAM at 7.6% of capacity). A differential expression benchmark at 3.4M cells showed pseudo-bulk aggregation 44x faster than cell-level t-test. We extended the benchmark to spatial transcriptomics on three 10x Visium platforms, achieving up to 51.6x end-to-end speedup (Visium HD 8 um) and 3,272x for co-occurrence analysis, with near-perfect spatial autocorrelation concordance (Spearman rho >= 0.9995). These results identify CPU-side preprocessing as the primary bottleneck and provide practical guidance for deploying GPU-accelerated workflows at atlas scale.
nuovo: **Abstract.** Single-cell and spatial transcriptomics now yield millions of cells or bins, yet standard frameworks run on CPUs. We compared rapids-singlecell on NVIDIA H100 GPUs with Scanpy on 100 logical CPUs of a DGX H100 node, on 10,000 to 1.3 million mouse brain cells sampled from CELLxGENE Census, five repeats each. At 1.3 million cells the GPU pipeline took 435 s against 52,056 s on CPU (119.6-fold; 105.5-fold with two GPUs allocated, a difference due to data loading alone). Wilcoxon differential expression accounted for 93.5% of the CPU time; without it the speedup was 7.9-9.2-fold. Additional GPUs did no computation in this configuration. At 10,000 cells, HVG selection was identical and Leiden clusterings agreed with ARI 0.908-0.963. A memory-optimised pipeline completed 11.9 million cells, built from copies of a 3,436,470-cell dataset; larger runs stopped at a Dask time-out or were killed in CPU preprocessing. At 3.4 million cells, pseudo-bulk differential expression took 127 s against 5,598 s for a cell-level t-test. For spatial data we rebuilt the CPU reference: one fresh process per repeat, the same cell groups for CPU and GPU. Against 100 CPUs of a DGX H100 node, an RTX 4090 accelerated end-to-end analysis 1.4-fold on Visium v1, 6.9-fold on Visium HD 8 um (without co-occurrence) and 10.4-fold on Visium HD 2 um. At Visium HD 8 um, GPU co-occurrence in rapids-singlecell 0.14.1 was wrong at 41 of 49 distances through 32-bit integer overflow; version 0.15.1 matched the CPU at all 49 in the same time.

vecchio: However, most benchmarks report headline speedups without systematically examining (i) per-step performance variation, (ii) multi-GPU scaling behaviour and its bottlenecks, (iii) numerical concordance of GPU floating-point results with CPU baselines, and (iv) practical memory limits at extreme scale.
nuovo: Earlier studies have reported per-step timings on one to eight GPUs with CPU-GPU concordance [@Nolet2022], a simulated 13-million-cell dataset processed on one A100 GPU [@Hu2025] and 100 million cells analysed on a node with eight GPUs [@Dicks2026].

vecchio: Gardner et al. [-@Gardner2025] recently evaluated accuracy-performance trade-offs for GPU single-cell analysis, but their study was limited to a single GPU and did not explore multi-GPU configurations or stress-test hardware limits.
nuovo:
Gardner et al. [-@Gardner2025] evaluated accuracy-performance trade-offs on NVIDIA H100 GPUs and found that CPU and GPU pipelines were not interchangeable (median ARI 0.45-0.55).
We complement these studies with three analyses: the share of the end-to-end speedup due to differential expression testing on one DGX H100 node, the largest cell count that a hybrid CPU-GPU pipeline completed on that node and where larger runs stopped, and a spatial benchmark of an RTX 4090 against a matched CPU reference.

vecchio: We benchmark both modalities on NVIDIA DGX H100 and RTX 4090 hardware, provide all code and containers for full reproducibility, and identify CPU-side preprocessing as the primary bottleneck limiting further scaling.
nuovo:
We ran the single-cell benchmark on an NVIDIA DGX H100 node and the spatial benchmark on an RTX 4090 workstation, both against 100 CPUs of a DGX H100 node, and we release the code, the container definitions and the per-run result files.
In this hybrid pipeline, the steps left on the CPU and the choice of differential expression test bounded the achievable speedup.
This chapter extends our CIBB 2026 short paper with a new CPU reference for the spatial benchmark, in which every repeat runs in a fresh process and CPU and GPU spatial statistics use the same cell groups; the new reference removes a slowdown of the CPU between repeats of the original spatial runs and shows that GPU co-occurrence at Visium HD 8 um was wrong because of 32-bit integer overflow, an error that rapids-singlecell 0.15.1 corrects.
